name: Modified Henry volar approach to the distal radius
corridor: Through FCR sheath, ulnar to radial artery, then between FPL and radial artery to pronator quadratus

positioning.text: Position supine with arm on radiolucent hand table, forearm supinated, and wrist extended over a small support.

setup.text: Mark FCR and radial artery, review lunate-facet and watershed-line anatomy, and prepare carpal-tunnel decompression as a separate or extensile option when indicated.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark FCR tendon, radial styloid, wrist crease, radial artery pulse, scaphoid tubercle, and palmaris longus when present.

incision.text: Incise longitudinally along the radial border of FCR, tailored to fracture and plate length.

superficial_interval.text: Open FCR sheath and retract tendon ulnarly while protecting the palmar cutaneous median-nerve branch on the ulnar side.

deep_interval.text: Develop between FPL and radial artery, sweep FPL ulnarly, and elevate pronator quadratus with an L-shaped incision whose distal limb stays near the watershed line.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous palmar-cutaneous nerve plane, FCR sheath, FPL-radial artery interval, pronator quadratus and periosteum, then volar radius.

structures_encountered.text: FCR, radial artery, palmar cutaneous median-nerve branch, FPL, pronator quadratus, volar capsule, and distal radius are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Palmar cutaneous median-nerve branch, median nerve proximally, radial artery, FPL, flexor tendons, and radiocarpal capsule are at risk.

danger_zones.text: The palmar cutaneous branch is most vulnerable distally and median nerve proximity increases proximally; remain in the defined FCR-based interval.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid prolonged radial-artery traction and excessive ulnar retraction of FPL and median nerve; use broad atraumatic retractors.

exposure.text: Exposes most volar distal-radius fractures and supports volar plate placement; it does not directly decompress the carpal tunnel.

limitations.text: Isolated lunate-facet, dorsal rim, and highly complex high-energy patterns may need ulnar-volar, dorsal, or combined approaches.

extensions.text: Extend proximally along FCR or add a separate carpal-tunnel, ulnar-volar, or dorsal exposure according to pathology.

indications.text: Use for most operatively treated distal-radius fractures amenable to volar reduction and plating.

relative_contraindications.text: Choose an alternative or combined approach when the critical fragment cannot be controlled volarly or volar skin is compromised.

implant_implications.text: Position the plate proximal to the watershed line when possible and confirm distal screws support subchondral bone without joint or dorsal-tendon penetration.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use PA, lateral, oblique, dorsal tangential, and tilted views to assess reduction, watershed position, and every distal screw.

closure.text: Reapproximate pronator quadratus over the plate when feasible, close FCR sheath only without trapping the palmar cutaneous nerve, then close skin.

complications.text: Complications include median or palmar-cutaneous neuropathy, radial-artery injury, flexor or extensor tendon irritation or rupture, joint penetration, stiffness, and hardware prominence.

bailouts.text: Add the required column-specific exposure when reduction remains unseen and decompress the carpal tunnel through an appropriate separate or extensile route when indicated.

procedure_applications.condition: Most volar-displaced or reducible distal-radius fractures require volar plate fixation

questions.question: What is the defining interval?
questions.answer: Between FCR and the radial artery, with the approach ulnar to the artery.

questions.question: Which nerve branch is at risk distally?
questions.answer: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve.

questions.question: Where is the distal pronator-quadratus limb placed?
questions.answer: At the watershed line a few millimeters proximal to the joint.
